lessons.title: Oral English: stress, intonation, sounds and rhyme
lessons.programRef: O Level English Language — oral English, listening and note-taking (to be checked against the official texts)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Place the stress in common words, including noun/verb pairs.
Use falling and rising intonation correctly.
Tell apart frequent vowel and consonant contrasts and recognise rhyme.
reviewNotes: Sounds are described by example words and in plain words, not with phonetic symbols. Pronunciation follows standard British English; a teacher or audio recording should confirm every example. Audio uses a text-to-speech voice that may not be perfect.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: Oral English tests **how words sound**, not how they are spelt. Practise **out loud**, listen to a model speaker (a radio newsreader or your teacher) and compare. The audio buttons in this lesson read the examples aloud.

blocks.text: Listen to these pairs. Ship, sheep. Bad, bed. Think, sink. Ship, chip. Light, right.

blocks.title: Word stress
blocks.md:
Every word of two or more syllables has one **stressed** syllable (said louder, longer, higher): *TAble, beGIN, eduCAtion, PHOtograph*.
- Some words change class with the stress: noun **REcord** / verb **reCORD**; noun **PREsent** / verb **preSENT**; noun **OBject** / verb **obJECT**.
- Words ending in **-tion, -sion, -ic, -ity** are stressed on the syllable **before** the ending: *eduCAtion, ecoNOMic, abilITy*.

items.text: Word stress: the big circle is the stressed syllable

blocks.caption: Mark the stress with capital letters.
blocks.alt: Two words. REcord as a noun with a big circle on the first syllable and a small one on the second. reCORD as a verb with a small circle then a big one.

blocks.title: Sentence stress and intonation
blocks.md:
- In a sentence we stress the **content words** (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs), not *the, a, of, to*: *I WANT to GO to MARket.*
- **Falling** intonation: statements, commands and *wh*- questions (*Where do you live?*).
- **Rising** intonation: yes/no questions (*Are you ready?*), and the items of a list before the last one; the last item falls.
- Moving the stress changes the meaning: *I did not take your pen* (somebody else did) / *I did not TAKE your pen* (I borrowed it).

items.text: Intonation: the voice falls or rises

blocks.caption: A wh- question falls; a yes/no question rises.
blocks.alt: Two lines. The blue line falls at the end of Where do you live. The orange line rises at the end of Are you ready.

blocks.title: Vowel and consonant contrasts
blocks.md:
- *ship* (short i) / *sheep* (long ee); *full* / *fool*.
- *bad* (a as in cat) / *bed* (e as in pen); *cup* (short u) / *cart* (long ah).
- *think* (tongue between the teeth) / *sink*; *this* / *dis*.
- *ship* (sh) / *chip* (ch); *light* / *right* (tongue position); *very* / *wary*; *bag* / *back*.
A minimal pair differs by **one sound** only: practise pairs aloud.

blocks.title: Rhyme, homophones and silent letters
blocks.md:
- Two words **rhyme** when they sound the same from the last stressed vowel: *cake – make*, *know – though – go*. Spelling can mislead: *cough* does not rhyme with *though*, and *bough* does not rhyme with *through*.
- **Homophones** sound the same but are spelt differently: *right / write, hear / here, their / there*.
- **Silent letters:** *knife, honest, wrist, island, climb*.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Stressing every syllable equally (a flat, « machine-gun » rhythm).
- Judging rhyme by **spelling**: *tough* and *though* do not rhyme.
- Raising the voice at the end of every sentence.
- Mixing the two *th* sounds with *t* or *d*, or *ship* with *sheep*.
- Putting the stress mark on the wrong syllable in a written exercise.

blocks.title: Example 1: the stress
blocks.statement: Mark the stressed syllable in: (a) begin (b) teacher (c) education.
steps: Two-syllable verbs often take the stress on the second syllable: **beGIN**; nouns on the first: **TEAcher**.
Words ending in -tion are stressed just before the ending: **eduCAtion**.

blocks.title: Example 2: rhyme
blocks.statement: Which word rhymes with *though*: (a) cough (b) go (c) through?
steps: Ignore the spelling and say the last sound: though = « thoh ».
Go = « goh »: same sound. Cough = « koff » and through = « throo ».

blocks.text: Where do you live? Are you ready? I want to go to market. Bring a pen, a ruler, and a notebook.

lessons.title: Listening and note-taking
lessons.programRef: O Level English Language — oral English, listening and note-taking (to be checked against the official texts)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Listen for key words: names, numbers, dates and places.
Use abbreviations and a clear layout when making notes.
reviewNotes: The audio block uses a text-to-speech voice; a teacher should preferably read the passages aloud. The abbreviation list is a suggestion.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: In listening tasks you hear a text **once or twice** and must write down the important points. You cannot write everything: **listen for key words** and write in **note form**. After listening you turn your notes into complete sentences.

blocks.text: Good morning, students. This is an announcement from the principal's office. The school sports day will take place on Thursday the fourteenth of May, not on Friday as announced earlier. Pupils should arrive at seven thirty in sports wear. Each class must bring two buckets of water and one first-aid box. Parents are invited and will sit under the tents near the football field. The first event is the one hundred metre race at eight o'clock.

items.text: Key words: who, what, when, where

blocks.caption: Write only the words you will need later.
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows: title or topic; key words who what when and where; exact numbers dates and names; signpost words like first, however and finally.

blocks.title: Before, during, after
blocks.md:
- **Before:** read the questions, predict what you will hear, and prepare a layout (headings or a grid).
- **During:** write **key words only**; use **abbreviations** and **symbols**; leave a space if you miss something; do not stop to think about one word.
- **After:** complete your notes at once, check numbers and names, and write answers in full sentences if asked.

blocks.title: Useful abbreviations
blocks.md:
- & = and; w/ = with; → = leads to / becomes; ↑ = increase; ↓ = decrease; no. = number; e.g. = for example.
- Days and months: *Thu, May*; money: *FCFA 2,000*; times: *7.30 am*.
- Use your own short forms if you can read them later. Write numbers as **digits**.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Trying to write every word and missing the next sentence.
- Writing the **wrong number** (fourteen / forty, thirteen / thirty): listen to the stress and the ending.
- Notes that you cannot read afterwards.
- Copying the speaker's wording instead of answering the exact question.
- Missing a **correction**: *Thursday, not Friday*.

blocks.title: Example 1: notes from the announcement
blocks.statement: Make notes from the announcement above (sports day).
steps: Title: **Sports Day**. Date: **Thu 14 May** (not Fri). Time: arrive **7.30 am**, first event **8.00 am** (100 m race).
Bring: **2 buckets of water + 1 first-aid box** per class. Dress: sports wear. Parents: invited, tents near the football field.
blocks.answer: Sports Day: Thu 14 May (not Fri); 7.30 arrive; sports wear; each class 2 buckets water + 1 first-aid box; parents invited; 8.00 100 m race.

blocks.title: Example 2: from notes to a sentence
blocks.statement: Write a sentence from the notes: *Thu 14 May (not Fri); 7.30 arrive; sports wear.*
steps: Use full words and the correct tense: this is an announcement about the future.
Include the correction: Thursday, not Friday.
blocks.answer: The sports day will take place on Thursday 14 May, not on Friday; pupils must arrive at 7.30 in sports wear.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt:
Listen (or read aloud): *Tomorrow the Red Cross will visit our school. Doctors will check the pupils' eyes from 9 a.m. in Room 3. Pupils from Form 1 to Form 3 go first. Pupils must bring their health booklets. The service is free.*
Make **notes** in note form (under 30 words), then write one full sentence from them.
exercises.model: Notes: Red Cross visit tomorrow; eye check 9 am Room 3; Forms 1-3 first; bring health booklet; free. Sentence: Tomorrow the Red Cross will check pupils' eyes free of charge from 9 a.m. in Room 3, and pupils must bring their health booklets.
rubric: 1 mark: the day, time and room.
1 mark: who goes first; what to bring; free.
1 mark: the notes are short (under 30 words).
exercises.explanation: Notes: Red Cross visit tomorrow; eye check 9 am Room 3; Forms 1-3 first; bring health booklet; free. Sentence: Tomorrow the Red Cross will check pupils' eyes free of charge from 9 a.m. in Room 3, and pupils must bring their health booklets.

exercises.prompt: In note-taking, a number should be written as...
exercises.explanation: Digits are quicker.

exercises.prompt: What should you do before the recording starts?
exercises.explanation: Predicting helps you listen for key words.

exercises.prompt: Notes should be written in...
exercises.explanation: Short form saves time.

exercises.prompt: Which is a signpost word?
exercises.explanation: It shows the order of ideas.

exercises.prompt: After listening you should...
exercises.explanation: Fill in the gaps while the memory is fresh.
